heading: C. Wright Mills, “The Promise”

works.cite: C. Wright Mills, “The Promise,” in The Sociological Imagination. Oxford University Press, 1959.

tie: Mills separates personal troubles, which happen inside one person's life, from public issues, which come from how a society is organized. He argues that people can only understand their own lives once they see that link.

A student who decides computer science "isn't for me" seems to be making a private choice. When the same choice shows up across whole groups of students, year after year, it is a public issue. This site treats enrollment, admissions and hiring numbers that way.

heading: Brown v. Board of Education and “The Problem We All Live With”

works.cite: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, 347 U.S. 483 (1954).
Nikole Hannah-Jones and Chana Joffe-Walt, “The Problem We All Live With,” Parts One and Two, This American Life, episodes 562 and 563, July 31 and Aug. 7, 2015.

idea: Access to a school is not the same as equal outcomes inside it
tie: Brown ruled that segregated public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause. Sixty years later, Nikole Hannah-Jones reported on the Normandy School District in Missouri, the district that includes Michael Brown's high school, where a transfer program opened better-resourced schools to its students and that access was fought over.

Stage 01 of the pipeline counts whether a school offers computer science. The rest of the diagram asks what happens after that door opens: who is placed in the class, who is pointed toward the AP exam and who reaches the next step. A course in the catalog is where the question starts, not where it ends.

heading: Bettina L. Love, “Grit, Zest, and Racism”

works.cite: Bettina L. Love, “Grit, Zest, and Racism,” in We Want to Do More Than Survive: Abolitionist Teaching and the Pursuit of Educational Freedom. Beacon Press, 2019.

idea: Don't blame students for dropping off
tie: Love argues that teaching grit asks students of color to endure conditions that racism created, and treats their survival as a character trait instead of changing the conditions.

When a dot falls off in the diagram, it is easy to read it as a student who didn't try hard enough. The log records where students leave, not why any one student did. The question at each stage is what about the school, the course or the policy pushed students out.

heading: Center on Education Policy, “For the Common Good,” and Milton Friedman, “The Role of Government in Education”

works.cite: Center on Education Policy, George Washington University, For the Common Good: Recommitting to Public Education in a Time of Crisis, 2020.
Milton Friedman, “The Role of Government in Education,” in Robert A. Solo, ed., Economics and the Public Interest. Rutgers University Press, 1955.

idea: Who education is for, and who should pay for it
tie: CEP argues that public schools serve public purposes, not only private ones, and makes the case for recommitting to a strong public system. Friedman argues that government is justified in paying for general education because an educated public benefits everyone, a "neighborhood effect," but not for "purely vocational education" that mainly raises one student’s earnings.

Most events on this timeline are arguments over that line. Supporters of the rollback say public money and public colleges should not favor some groups over others. The programs being cut were built on the idea that widening who studies computer science is a public good, not only a private investment.

heading: This course is taught under Senate Bill 1

works.cite: ESPHE 3206 (School & Society) course syllabus, The Ohio State University, “Intellectual Diversity” section.

tie: The ESPHE 3206 syllabus cites Senate Bill 1 under Intellectual Diversity. SB 1 requires Ohio State and every other state university to post course syllabi publicly and to "ensure the fullest degree of intellectual diversity."
The rollback on this page is not only something that happens at other schools. It shapes how this course, the one this site was made for, describes itself.

heading: Richard Rothstein, Class and Schools

works.cite: Richard Rothstein, Class and Schools: Using Social, Economic, and Educational Reform to Close the Black-White Achievement Gap. Economic Policy Institute and Teachers College, Columbia University, 2004.

idea: Social class shapes what students bring to school
tie: Rothstein argues that achievement gaps grow out of social class differences outside school, in income, health, housing and early childhood, and that closing them takes social and economic policy as well as school reform.

A high school computer science course meets students who arrive with very different amounts of exposure to computing. Offering the course, stage 01 of the pipeline, does not undo what happened before a student walked in.

heading: bell hooks, “Confronting Class in the Classroom”

works.cite: bell hooks, “Confronting Class in the Classroom,” in Teaching to Transgress: Education as the Practice of Freedom. Routledge, 1994.

idea: The silence about class in classrooms
tie: hooks writes that class is rarely talked about in American classrooms, and that middle-class values quietly set the terms for how students are expected to speak and behave.

In a computer science classroom, those unspoken terms can include assuming that students already own a computer or have written code before. Students who don’t fit those assumptions can read them as a sign that the class isn’t for them.

heading: Mahzarin R. Banaji and Anthony G. Greenwald, “Mindbugs”

works.cite: Mahzarin R. Banaji and Anthony G. Greenwald, “Mindbugs,” in Blindspot: Hidden Biases of Good People. Delacorte Press, 2013.

idea: Implicit bias in who gets recommended
tie: Banaji and Greenwald use “mindbugs” for ingrained habits of thought that lead well-meaning people into errors of perception and judgment, often without noticing.

A recommendation for AP is a quick judgment made many times a year. In the Francis study the transcripts were identical, so the only thing that changed was the name, and the name changed the recommendation.

heading: Elliot W. Eisner, “Questionable Assumptions About Schooling”

works.cite: Elliot W. Eisner, “Questionable Assumptions About Schooling,” Phi Delta Kappan 84, no. 9 (2003): 648–657.

idea: Tracking as part of how school is assumed to work
tie: Eisner questions the assumption that school should move every student to the same place at about the same time, a race run “on a track for which their life experiences have advantaged them.” He asks readers to examine structures that are taken for granted, including how classes are organized.

Grade cutoffs and counselor sign-offs for AP are that kind of structure. They feel neutral because they are routine, yet Hirschl and Smith found they open racial gaps among students with similar records.

heading: Anne Sisson Runyan, “What Is Intersectionality and Why Is It Important?”

works.cite: Anne Sisson Runyan, “What Is Intersectionality and Why Is It Important?” Academe, November–December 2018.

idea: Why the gaps are not simply added together
tie: Runyan traces intersectionality to Kimberlé Crenshaw and stresses that forms of oppression are “not just additive.” Women of color face a different form of racism than men of color, and a different form of sexism than white women.

That is what the Francis study found: counselors were least likely to recommend Black female students, a gap that looking at race alone or gender alone would miss. For low-income women of color, class shapes those gaps too.

heading: Brown v. Board of Education and “The Problem We All Live With”

works.cite: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, 347 U.S. 483 (1954).
Nikole Hannah-Jones and Chana Joffe-Walt, “The Problem We All Live With,” Parts One and Two, This American Life, episodes 562 and 563, July 31 and Aug. 7, 2015.

idea: The history this ruling sits in
tie: Both sides in SFFA claimed Brown. The majority read it as a rule against any use of race: “The time for making distinctions based on race had passed.” Justice Sotomayor’s dissent argued that race-conscious admissions “promoted Brown’s vision of a Nation with more inclusive schools.”

Six decades after Brown, This American Life introduced Nikole Hannah-Jones’s reporting by noting that desegregation is the one thing “nobody tries anymore, despite lots of evidence that it works.” The fall 2025 numbers on this page are an early look at selective colleges once race can no longer be considered at all.
notes: Majority quote: SFFA v. Harvard, opinion of the Court, slip op. at 13. Dissent quote: Sotomayor, J., dissenting, slip op. at 2. Desegregation quote: This American Life, episode 562 description, July 31, 2015.

heading: Richard Rothstein, Class and Schools

works.cite: Richard Rothstein, Class and Schools: Using Social, Economic, and Educational Reform to Close the Black-White Achievement Gap. Economic Policy Institute and Teachers College, Columbia University, 2004.
Lewis Diuguid, “Addressing Classism Will Improve School Performance,” The Kansas City Star, Jan. 17, 2006, reposted by Teachers College.

idea: Why class-based admissions alone does not close racial gaps
tie: Rothstein argues that the Black-white achievement gap grows out of social and economic conditions that schools alone can’t change. “You can’t fix it with school reform,” he told the Kansas City Star. “The biggest improvements will come when you address social and economic inequality.”

Class-based admissions uses income as the measure of disadvantage. The national study in this section found evidence that Ivy Plus colleges pivoted toward class-based admissions after SFFA, yet the share of Black, Hispanic, Native American and Pacific Islander students at highly selective colleges still fell 4 to 5 percentage points. Income and race are linked, but one does not stand in for the other.

heading: James W. Loewen, “Handicapped by History: The Process of Hero-Making”

works.cite: James W. Loewen, “Handicapped by History: The Process of Hero-Making,” chapter 1 in Lies My Teacher Told Me: Everything Your American History Textbook Got Wrong. The New Press, 1995.

idea: Who shows up as a computer scientist in what students learn
tie: Loewen argues that textbooks turn people into simple heroes by leaving out what makes them complicated, such as Helen Keller’s socialism or Woodrow Wilson’s racism. What gets left out shapes what students think is possible.

Computer science has hero stories too. When the people students hear about are mostly the same kind of person, students learn what a computer scientist is supposed to look like long before anyone hires them. Company diversity reports were one of the few public places a different picture showed up, and they are going away.

heading: David Takacs, “How Does Your Positionality Bias Your Epistemology?”

works.cite: David Takacs, “How Does Your Positionality Bias Your Epistemology?” Thought & Action (NEA Higher Education Journal), Summer 2003.

idea: Where you stand shapes what you can see
tie: Takacs asks readers to notice how their own position, the identities and experiences they bring, shapes what they accept as true. He argues that admitting your views are not inevitable makes you more open to other people’s knowledge.
This site is written from inside one student chapter. That position shows some things clearly and hides others, which is why the page leaves room for who was still missing.

heading: Jane Margolis and Allan Fisher, Unlocking the Clubhouse

works.cite: Jane Margolis and Allan Fisher, Unlocking the Clubhouse: Women in Computing. MIT Press, 2002.

idea: Why students leave after they get in
tie: Interviewing more than 100 Carnegie Mellon computer science students, Margolis and Fisher found women leaving the major after they had been admitted because its culture eroded their confidence, not because they were less interested or able.
Student-run communities answer that problem from the ground up: a place where students who don’t match the default picture of a computer scientist find peers doing the same work.
